analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to cover mental illness on the same terms as physical illness.
analysis.headline: With 231 of 435 House members signed on as cosponsors, the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped employer health plans from charging higher copays, imposing stricter visit caps, or setting lower annual and lifetime limits for mental health care than they do for physical care. It applied only to plans that already offer mental health benefits, and it exempted employers with 50 or fewer employees. Plans would still have been free to manage mental health care with preauthorization and network rules, as long as the same rules applied to physical care.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-sponsored insurance who need mental health treatment. They would no longer face higher cost sharing, tighter limits on the number of therapy visits or hospital days, or mental-health-only annual and lifetime caps, since any limit would have to match what the plan applies to medical and surgical care [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and families using mental health care

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans from imposing treatment limits or cost sharing on mental health benefits unless comparable limits apply to medical and surgical benefits, including deductibles, coinsurance, and annual and lifetime caps [S2] [S3].

Allows plans to keep using medical management tools like preauthorization and provider networks for mental health care, as long as the same tools are used for physical care, so the bill sets equal treatment rather than mandating any specific services [S3].
Exempts small employers with 2 to 50 employees, leaving them out of the requirement entirely [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor large group plans, who would face higher claims costs when mental health care is no longer cheaper to restrict than physical care. Some of that cost would flow to all enrollees through premiums, and the CRS summary notes the GAO was directed to study effects on insurance costs [S2].

drawbacks.text: Opponents of mental health parity have long argued that requiring equal coverage raises premiums for everyone in a plan, and the bill itself directs the GAO to study its effects on health insurance costs, an acknowledgment that cost was a real question [S2] [S3].

Plans can avoid the mandate entirely by not offering mental health benefits, since nothing in the bill requires a plan to provide them — so an employer wanting to escape the cost could drop the benefit rather than equalize it [S3].
Small employers with up to 50 workers are exempt, so many employees at smaller firms would have gotten no protection from the bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of people whose coverage the bill would have changed, the gain is substantial: mental health care that costs more out of pocket or runs out after a fixed number of visits is the main reason many people go without treatment. The cost — somewhat higher premiums spread across a plan's enrollees — is real but modest compared to the burden parity removes, and the bill was deliberately narrowed (small employer exemption, no substance abuse mandate, no requirement to offer any mental health benefit) to limit that cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees without ever getting a markup or a vote; the sponsor tried to force it to the floor with a discharge petition, which failed to collect enough signatures before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Kennedy of Rhode Island, joined by Rep. Jim Ramstad, introduced the bill on March 17, 2005 [S3].
The Speaker referred it to two committees — Education and the Workforce and Energy and Commerce — meaning it needed to move in both before reaching the floor [S5].
Within a week it was sent to subcommittees in both committees, and no markup or vote ever followed [S5].

More than a year later, on September 28, 2006, Kennedy filed a discharge petition — a device that requires 218 House member signatures to pull a bill out of committee and force a floor vote — but the petition never succeeded and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and large employers came out ahead: the parity requirement never took effect, so plans could keep limiting mental health benefits more tightly than physical care. People with mental illness who relied on employer coverage kept paying the difference.

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and later filed a discharge petition to pull it out of committee for a floor vote [S3] [S5].

for.name: Rep. Jim Ramstad
for.what_they_did: Joined Kennedy in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship [S3].

for.name: 231 House cosponsors (39 Republicans, 191 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, a majority of the House, without the bill ever reaching the floor [S4].

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill and referred it to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it sat with no markup for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Rep. Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill and referred it to the Health Subcommittee, where it never advanced [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: With the bill held in committee, no floor consideration was ever scheduled despite a majority of the House signed on as cosponsors [S4] [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 231 cosponsors including 39 Republicans and the bill's co-introducer Jim Ramstad, a Republican — but no vote was ever taken, so the opposition never had to register on the record.

industries.note: Parity would force plans to apply the same copays, visit limits, and dollar caps to mental health care as to physical care, raising their claims costs. Plans could also escape the rule by dropping mental health coverage altogether, which the bill permits [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Large employers offering group health plans
industries.note: Employers with more than 50 employees would face higher premiums as benefits equalized; smaller employers were explicitly exempted [S2] [S3].
With cost sharing and visit limits equalized, more patients could afford therapy and psychiatric care, and providers would face fewer arbitrary caps on treatment [S2] [S3].
